pieces.title: He drew orbits for the atom, then admitted the picture wasn't enough: Niels Bohr
pieces.hook: Offer a picture that works, then have the courage to admit it falls short: Bohr did not treat his 1913 orbit picture as…
pieces.takeaway: Offer a picture that works, then have the courage to admit it falls short: Bohr did not treat his 1913 orbit picture as the finish line, but turned it into the starting point for further discussion.
pieces.imageCredit: AB Lagrelius & Westphal (Stockholm) · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Niels Bohr (1885–1962) was a Danish physicist. He was born in Copenhagen on 7 October 1885. His father was a professor of physiology; his mother came from a banking family.
Four days from now, on 18 November, is the 64th anniversary of his death.

In 1911 he finished his doctoral thesis in Copenhagen, went to Cambridge, then moved on to Manchester and joined Rutherford's laboratory. The atomic model of the time had electrons circling a nucleus — but by classical electromagnetism they should keep radiating energy and quickly fall into the nucleus.

In 1913 Bohr published three papers in a row, proposing that electrons can only sit in certain "stationary states", and give off or absorb light only when they jump between states. For the first time, the pattern in the hydrogen spectrum had a clear explanation.

【An institute built on beer money】In 1916 he became a professor at the University of Copenhagen. On 3 March 1921 the Institute for Theoretical Physics officially opened, with major funding from the Carlsberg Foundation and others. He led it for decades; Heisenberg, Pauli, Dirac and many others worked there or made long visits.
In 1922 he won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on atomic structure and radiation. His son Aage also became a physicist and won a Nobel Prize in 1975.

The Bohr model soon stopped being enough. Once quantum mechanics was established, he proposed "complementarity" in 1927: wave and particle, position and momentum, cannot all be told at once with one set of classical pictures. For more than a decade afterwards, he and Einstein argued again and again — at the Solvay conferences and elsewhere — over whether quantum theory was complete.

Einstein wanted a more definite description; Bohr held that the existing theory already gave everything experiments could test. Neither convinced the other, and the debate itself became one of the most famous conversations in 20th-century science.

In 1939, with Wheeler and others, he explained the mechanism of nuclear fission and pointed out the key difference between uranium-235 and uranium-238. Germany occupied Denmark in 1940. In 1943, because of his mother's Jewish ancestry and the risk of arrest, he fled by boat to Sweden, then went on to Britain and the United States, where he advised the Manhattan Project under the alias Nicholas Baker.
Late in the war he urged Roosevelt and other leaders to place nuclear weapons under international control, so that the post-war world would not slide into an arms race.

paras.lead: An open letter to the United Nations
parts: In 1950 he published an open letter to the United Nations, again calling for openness and international cooperation. In 1957 he received the first Atoms for Peace Award. He died in Copenhagen on 18 November 1962, aged 77.
Later, element 107 was named bohrium after him.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Bohr｜View: A new theory must explain experiments, and also admit the limits of classical intuition.；Interest: Build an open international research centre.；Worry: That the quantum debate is misunderstood, and that nuclear knowledge feeds an uncontrolled arms race.；Basis: The 1913 model; complementarity in 1927; the 1950 open letter to the UN.

Einstein｜View: A physical description should be more complete than probabilities.；Interest: Preserve a clear picture of causality and reality.；Worry: Treating "cannot be measured precisely at the same time" as the final shape of the world.；Basis: His repeated challenges at the Solvay conferences; the later EPR argument.

Young physicists in Copenhagen｜View: Push the mathematics and the experiments forward through argument.；Interest: Do their own work alongside Bohr.；Worry: Being tied to one "official interpretation".；Basis: The work of Heisenberg, Pauli and others at the institute; the "Copenhagen interpretation" is in fact a later summary.

The wartime US and British governments｜View: Build the weapon first, discuss the international order later.；Interest: End the war quickly and keep a technological edge.；Worry: Secrecy being broken.；Basis: Bohr took part as an adviser; his call for international control did not become policy at the time.

Denmark and the post-war scientific community｜View: A small country can still be a crossroads of world physics.；Interest: Scientific reputation and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.；Worry: Talent and agendas being pulled into great-power military programmes.；Basis: Funding for the institute from Carlsberg and others; Bohr's Atoms for Peace Award.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: He helped people understand fission, and worried earlier than many colleagues about its political consequences.
His opposition to Einstein actually made the meaning of quantum theory clearer, time after time.
The institute attracted talent through openness; the war forced that openness to pause.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: He always held that quantum mechanics was complete; later experiments confirmed the strangeness of quantum entanglement, but there is still no agreed answer on "how to understand it".

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Accounts of Heisenberg's 1941 conversation with Bohr differ widely between the two men and later stage plays; this article does not invent the dialogue.
The "Copenhagen interpretation" is a label packaged by later writers; Bohr himself spoke more often of complementarity.
Public records of the exact scope of his technical contribution to the Manhattan Project are limited.

pieces.title: First it lit up a small town, then it learned to be afraid: seventy years of nuclear power
pieces.hook: On 27 June 1954, the experimental nuclear power station at Obninsk in the Soviet Union began sending electricity to the grid.
pieces.imageAlt: The former Obninsk nuclear power station
pieces.imageCredit: Pavel Bykov（RIA Novosti） · CC BY-SA 3.0，Wikimedia Commons

parts: On 27 June 1954, the experimental nuclear power station at Obninsk in the Soviet Union began sending electricity to the grid. For the first time, controlled nuclear fission became the light in a light bulb. Ten years earlier, the same physics had entered history as a weapon.
From the very start, nuclear power has walked between "clean baseload electricity" and "something that, if it goes wrong, can't be handled like an ordinary factory".

On 2 December 1942, Fermi and his colleagues built the first controlled chain-reacting pile in Chicago. After the war, countries turned reactors toward generating power. In 1956 Britain's Calder Hall station began operating, often called the first industrial-scale commercial nuclear power station; in 1957 the Shippingport station in the US was connected to the grid.
The early units were small; what mattered was proving that fission heat could turn water into steam and drive a turbine generator.

Mainland China's first nuclear power station was Qinshan in Zhejiang: its first unit was connected to the grid on 15 December 1991. The two units at Daya Bay in Guangdong entered commercial operation in 1994 — larger in scale, and bringing in more foreign cooperation and commercial operating experience.

From there, China's nuclear industry grew outward from the coast, gradually forming a series built mainly on pressurised-water reactors, and became one of the countries with the most reactors under construction.

paras.lead: Three plants that changed public opinion
parts: In 1979 the Three Mile Island accident in the US showed the public, up close, that a reactor core could partly melt down, even though off-site radioactive releases were limited. On 26 April 1986 the Chernobyl accident caused widespread contamination and long-term health and social consequences; estimates of deaths and long-term effects still differ greatly.

On 11 March 2011, after an earthquake and tsunami, Japan's Fukushima Daiichi plant lost power and melted down, again putting disaster-proof design, evacuation and contaminated-water treatment centre stage. After these three accidents, many countries slowed, paused or even abandoned nuclear power, and safety standards and costs rose sharply.

putting the climate account and the safety account side by side】According to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), at the end of 2025 there were 413 nuclear reactors in operation worldwide, with about 377.1 gigawatts of capacity. Nuclear plants emit almost no carbon dioxide directly while running and can generate continuously, so in climate debates some people again see them as necessary; opponents stress accident risk, spent-fuel storage, long build times and cost overruns.

New designs such as small modular reactors raise hopes, but most are not yet commercial at scale. The future of nuclear power no longer depends only on whether it can generate electricity, but on whether society is willing to pay for this kind of risk.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Nuclear operators and equipment makers｜View: Nuclear power can provide stable, low-carbon baseload electricity.；Interest: Long-term power revenue and orders across the supply chain.；Worry: Construction delays, rising costs, shutdowns and claims after accidents.；Basis: Early demonstration plants connected to the grid successfully; many later projects ran badly over budget.

Governments and regulators｜View: They need energy security and emission cuts, and must also prevent uncontrollable disasters.；Interest: Power supply, climate targets and public safety.；Worry: Accountability for accidents and public backlash.；Basis: Safety standards were tightened after accidents; policy has swung back and forth across decades.

Nearby residents and anti-nuclear groups｜View: The risk is highly concentrated while the benefits are shared much more widely.；Interest: The safety of lives, land and the food chain.；Worry: Too little information is disclosed and evacuation plans exist only on paper.；Basis: Large-scale evacuations and decontamination after Chernobyl and Fukushima.

Supporters of climate policy｜View: Without nuclear, emission cuts will rely more on the weather and on storage that is not yet mature.；Interest: Cut carbon emissions from the power system as fast as possible.；Worry: New nuclear plants are too slow to keep up with emission timetables.；Basis: Near-zero direct carbon emissions during operation; new builds often take a decade.

Spent fuel and reprocessing｜View: Waste must be treated as an engineering problem, not a slogan.；Interest: Safe storage and possible recycling.；Worry: Sites for final disposal are extremely hard to get accepted.；Basis: Most countries still rely on temporary or interim storage; permanent disposal is moving slowly.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The probability of an accident is argued to be very low, but when one happens the cost crosses borders and generations.
Stricter safety standards raised confidence, but also pushed costs to levels many projects cannot bear.
Climate goals brought nuclear power back to the table, but the waste and siting problems did not disappear.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: The hardest part of nuclear power is not whether it can run, but how long a society will keep agreeing to carry this low-probability, high-impact risk.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Estimates of the total deaths and illnesses linked to Chernobyl vary widely between agencies and studies.

Global reactor and capacity counts change with how "operating / long-term shutdown" is defined; this article uses the IAEA's "operating" count; the World Nuclear Association counts "operable" reactors, which gives higher numbers.
The commercial prospects of small modular reactors are still forecasts and cannot be treated as accomplished fact.

pieces.title: More money moved, less charged on each transfer: Wise's half-year accounts
pieces.hook: At 4 pm US Eastern time on 12 November (early on the 13th, Beijing time), cross-border money-transfer company …
pieces.event: 2026-11-12 (New York): first-half FY2027 results released after the US market close; London shares rose 7.68% on 11-13
pieces.imageCredit: Estonian Ministry of Foreign Affairs · CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

parts: At 4 pm US Eastern time on 12 November (early on the 13th, Beijing time), the cross-border money-transfer company Wise reported results for the half-year to 30 September, the first half of its 2027 financial year: net revenue of $1.4531 billion, up 23% from a year earlier; customers sent a total of $141 billion abroad through it, up 24%. The next day, its London shares last traded at 894.40 pence, up 7.68% on the previous close.

In January 2011, two Estonians working in London — Taavet Hinrikus, an early Skype employee, and Kristo Käärmann, a Deloitte consultant — founded TransferWise. Hinrikus found that when sending money between Estonia and the UK, banks usually took at least 5%, and most of the cost was hidden in the exchange rate where you couldn't see it.

Their approach was to exchange money at the mid-market rate and show the fee separately and openly. The company renamed itself Wise in February 2021 and listed directly on the London Stock Exchange that July; in May 2026 it also listed on Nasdaq in the US, becoming dual-listed.

paras.lead: More money moved, less charged on each transfer
parts: To read these accounts, first meet one number: the take rate — how much Wise charges, on average, for every $100 a customer sends. In the first half it was 0.50%, against 0.52% a year earlier, a drop of 0.02 percentage points.

For personal customers it fell from 0.57% to 0.55%, for business customers from 0.39% to 0.38%. So while transfer volume rose 24%, cross-border revenue rose only 19%, to $705 million. The company says this was deliberate: it passed part of the cost savings from growing scale on to customers, to "further strengthen our competitive advantage of lower prices".

Cross-border revenue now makes up just under half of net revenue (about 48.5%). Another part is cards: customers spent $27.2 billion on Wise cards, up 33%, and card revenue was $252 million, up 43%, mainly from business customers in the US.

Then there is interest: customers keep $32.1 billion in balances at Wise, up 22%; the company invests it and earned $463.6 million in interest, of which $112.7 million was paid back to customers. Interest income grew only 16%, slower than balances, because average yields were lower than last year.

【Revenue up 23%, profit up only 9%】The reason is faster spending. Total operating expenses were $1.1503 billion, up 28%: technology and development $292.2 million, up 51%, spent on new products, cloud services and a second data site; customer service and compliance $250.6 million, up 40%; marketing $111.7 million, up 46%; general and administrative costs $256.7 million, up 41%, including about $15 million of one-off costs for the US listing.

The only cost that fell was transaction expenses, down 12% to $229.7 million, thanks to better terms negotiated with partners. In the end, profit before tax was $334.9 million, up 9%, a 23% margin; net income was $249.2 million, up 6%.

The market cared more about what the company said for the full year. Wise expects FY2027 net revenue to grow 17.5% to 20% at constant currency, the upper half of its 15–20% medium-term target, and a full-year pre-tax margin around the top of its 20–25% range.

In addition, the share buyback that began in July is expected to exceed $500 million and is almost half done. According to Investing.com, the London shares rose as much as 9.6% during the day before easing back.

Revenue, take rate, costs and the full-year outlook all come from Wise's 12 November results announcement; the share price comes from Global Banking & Finance Review's after-close data and is the last traded price, not the exchange's official close. "Cutting prices is a deliberate investment" is the company's own description.

A 23% margin in the first half but close to 25% for the full year implies a higher margin in the second half — this is an inference from the company's guidance, not its own words. All of the above describes facts and market reactions that have already happened; it is not a view on the share price.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Management｜View: Low prices are the moat; part of the savings from scale should go to customers.；Interest: Gain share, and get more people and businesses to keep money in and send money with Wise.；Worry: Investing too hard, so costs eat up profit growth.；Basis: 12 November announcement: the 2-basis-point cut in the take rate was a "proactive investment of part of our operating leverage"; CEO Käärmann says 78% of transfers now arrive instantly and the average fee is only 0.50%.

Shareholders｜View: As long as the full-year margin holds, trading lower prices for growth is acceptable.；Interest: Profit, buybacks and the share price.；Worry: Costs (up 28%) growing faster than revenue (up 23%) for a long time.；Basis: London shares up 7.68% on 11-13 (Global Banking & Finance Review); Investing.com: up as much as 9.6% intraday, while noting pre-tax profit grew only 9%.

Personal and business customers｜View: Cross-border transfers should be cheap, fast and easy to see through.；Interest: Lower fees, faster arrival, one account for many currencies.；Worry: Fees hidden in the exchange rate — exactly the old problem the company was founded to solve.；Basis: Business transfer volume $43.6 billion, up 35%; personal $97.5 billion, up 19% (announcement); Hinrikus has said banks took at least 5%, mostly hidden in the rate (as cited by Wikipedia).

Banks｜View: Building global rails yourself is too expensive; better to plug into Wise's system.；Interest: Offer their own customers cheap cross-border transfers.；Worry: Handing key infrastructure to a company that is also competing for their customers.；Basis: Announcement: Wise Platform added OakNorth in the UK, Vivid in Europe and two of the top 20 North American banks, and expanded its services to Morgan Stanley.

Regulators｜View: Cross-border money flows must be guarded against money laundering and fraud.；Interest: Financial stability and consumer protection.；Worry: The company expanding faster than its compliance can keep up.；Basis: Announcement: servicing and compliance costs up 40%; its Belgian subsidiary settled inquiries from the Brussels prosecutor with no admission of wrongdoing; financial crime and fraud listed as a principal risk.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The company wants to win the market with lower prices, shareholders want to see margins; full-year guidance near 25% is the number both sides could accept this time.
Banks are both rivals and customers: the cheaper Wise gets, the more banks want to plug into it — and the more they worry about being replaced by it.
The more products and countries, the bigger the compliance and technology spending, and this cost is hard to shrink with scale.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: How much further the take rate can fall, and whether interest income shrinks as rates come down — these two decide whether Wise can stay cheap and still make money; the announcement gives no longer-term answer.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The share price of 894.40 pence, up 7.68%, is the last traded price after the close, not the London Stock Exchange's official close; the day's Nasdaq performance was not checked for this article.
"Price cuts are a deliberate investment" and "78% of transfers arrive instantly" are the company's figures and have not been verified by a third party.
The need for a higher second-half margin is inferred from full-year guidance; the company did not give separate second-half figures.

pieces.title: A former prime minister goes home to serve his sentence, and a minister resigns: a crack in Malaysia's ruling coalition
pieces.short: A crack in Malaysia's ruling coalition
pieces.hook: Around 9:30 pm on 10 November, Malaysia's former prime minister Najib Razak rode in a convoy escorted by police…
pieces.event: 2026-11-10 (Kuala Lumpur): Najib moved to house arrest, Anthony Loke resigned as transport minister; Melaka state election on 11-14, result not yet known at press time

parts: Around 9:30 pm on 10 November, Malaysia's former prime minister Najib Razak rode in a convoy escorted by police from Kajang Prison to his home in Taman Duta, Kuala Lumpur, to begin serving his sentence under "house arrest". Under the court's order that day, he must stay at home until 23 August 2028 and may not leave without permission.

That same afternoon, Transport Minister Anthony Loke issued a statement resigning with immediate effect. He is secretary-general of the Democratic Action Party (DAP), the party with the most seats in parliament within the governing Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition.

Najib was prime minister from 2009 to 2018. In August 2022 the Federal Court upheld his conviction for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering in the case of SRC International, a former subsidiary of the state fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB); he was sentenced to 12 years and went to prison.

In 2024 the Pardons Board halved his sentence to six years and cut his fine from RM210 million to RM50 million. In December 2025 he was sentenced to another 15 years in the main 1MDB case, which he is appealing.

On 18 September 2026, the King, Sultan Ibrahim, granted Najib a conditional pardon: once the fine was paid, he could serve the rest of his sentence at home. His party, UMNO, ran a crowdfunding campaign and paid the RM50 million (about US$12.3 million) on 6 November.

He left prison that day, but was taken back a few hours later: the Attorney-General asked the court to clarify first whether this meant his first sentence had been completed — which decides when the 15 years in the 1MDB case start. The palace then said publicly that the power of pardon is given to the King by Article 42 of the Constitution, and that with all conditions met, disputing the order "would amount to defying the command of His Majesty".
The Attorney-General's Chambers replied that it was not disputing the pardon. On 10 November, High Court judge Aslam Zainuddin set aside the 6 November order and issued a new one.

As early as 19 September, Loke had said that if Najib was allowed to serve his sentence at home, he would resign; on 28 September he handed his resignation letter to Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, to take effect on the day Najib went home. He said it was a party decision, meant to express disagreement with this conditional pardon.

The DAP's four other ministers stayed, saying they would remain to finish unfinished reforms. On 13 November Anwar told reporters he had "not accepted the resignation yet", would take time to review it carefully, and "there is no need for us to rush".

At the federal level, Anwar's PH and the UMNO-led Barisan Nasional (BN) sit together in a "unity government". Yet UMNO paid Najib's fine, while the DAP used a resignation to object. On 11 November Anwar wrote on Facebook: "Those of us who hate and oppose corruption need to speak out more forcefully … those who commit corruption belong in prison.

" He has also said he disagreed with UMNO paying someone's fine. Deputy Prime Minister and UMNO president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi used the moment to call for an early general election: "There is no need to reshuffle the Cabinet as it is better to dissolve Parliament and return the mandate to the voters." The current parliament must face an election by early 2028 at the latest.

On Saturday 14 November, Melaka votes for the 28 seats in its state assembly — Anwar's third electoral test this year. In the outgoing assembly, BN held 20 seats and PH only five. Partners at the federal level, PH and BN are rivals here: BN has teamed up with the opposition Perikatan Nasional (PN, led by the Islamic party PAS), contesting 23 and 5 seats respectively; PH is contesting 24; Bersama, the new party of former economy minister Rafizi Ramli, 16; and Bersatu, which recently agreed to back Anwar's government through a confidence-and-supply arrangement, 7.
Zahid has said that if BN and PN win, the two blocs will form the state government together. At press time (early on 14 November, Beijing time), voting had not yet begun.

blocks.title: How the "unity government" came about
blocks.text: After the November 2022 general election, no side held a majority of parliament's 222 seats. After the King stepped in, Anwar's PH and its old rival BN, among others, formed a coalition government, with Anwar as prime minister. Allies at the federal level, they are still rivals in state elections — which is why, in the same week, the two sides sat in one cabinet while criticising each other from campaign stages in Melaka.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Prime Minister Anwar and PH｜View: The anti-corruption stance stays, but the government must be kept stable first.；Interest: Hold on until the 2028 election and get the newly announced budget delivered.；Worry: The DAP drifting away, and UMNO using the moment to push him out.；Basis: 11-11 Facebook post saying the corrupt belong in prison; 11-13 said he had not accepted the resignation and there was "no need to rush" (Malay Mail, CNA).

DAP and Anthony Loke｜View: They cannot stay silent on the conditional pardon.；Interest: Keep supporters' expectations that the party fights corruption.；Worry: Staying in government looks like compromise, while leaving entirely could destabilise it.；Basis: Public statements since September; the 11-10 resignation statement cited his earlier "principles and stand"; the other four ministers stay (CNA).

UMNO and BN｜View: Najib going home is royal clemency and should be respected.；Interest: Rally supporters, win more seats in Melaka, push for an early election.；Worry: Being criticised for backing a man convicted of corruption.；Basis: UMNO crowdfunded and paid the RM50 million; Zahid called for dissolving parliament on 11-10 (The Edge); UMNO vice-president Mohamad Hasan said Loke's resignation questioned the King's power of pardon (CNA).

The palace and the Attorney-General's Chambers｜View: Palace: the power of pardon must be respected; AGC: first clarify in law how the two sentences fit together.；Interest: Palace: uphold the power of pardon under constitutional monarchy; AGC: avoid future disputes over when a sentence starts.；Worry: That the disagreement is read as a clash between the monarchy and the government.；Basis: Sultan Ibrahim's statement citing Article 42 of the Constitution; the AGC said it was not disputing the pardon and applied to the High Court for a new order (CNA, The Star).

Melaka voters and observers｜View: Use their votes to say what they think of these disputes.；Interest: Who forms the state government.；Worry: Ethnic voting becoming even more polarised.；Basis: International Islamic University scholar Tunku Mohar: Najib's house arrest and the BN–PN pact "could polarise ethnic voters further"; he also thinks Anwar still has enough numbers in parliament (The Edge).

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: UMNO is Anwar's partner at the federal level but has joined forces with the opposition PN in Melaka; the same people sit together in cabinet while fighting each other on campaign stages.
By having one minister resign in protest while four stay to keep the government going, the DAP is balancing between "taking a stand" and "not letting the government fall".
Anwar's lack of hurry to accept the resignation leaves the DAP a way back, and also gives UMNO grounds for its line that dissolving parliament beats a reshuffle.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Anwar still has enough votes in parliament, but the two main partners in his cabinet take opposite positions on the same issue; whether Melaka's ballots turn this crack into pressure for an early election must wait for tonight's result.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The Melaka election result was not out at press time; this article makes no prediction.
There are reports of a minor reshuffle involving DAP ministers (FMT); at press time the cabinet line-up had not formally changed.

On when the 15-year 1MDB sentence starts: the AGC's application specified a transfer back to Kajang Prison on 24 August 2028, but reports differ on whether the court's new order explicitly includes this.
